newsitem.title: TAIWAN: YEAREND-Taiwan's China investments sags in 1996.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Taiwan's China investments sags in 1996.

text.p: It has not been a good year for Taiwan investors eager to enter the huge potential market in mainland China.

Relations between Taiwan and China, rivals since a civil war ended in 1949, have been mired since Beijing mobilised its armed forces for intimidating war games before Taiwan's first direct presidential election in March.
China, which sees the Nationalist-ruled island as a rebel-held province, acknowledged the aim of the manoeuvres and missile tests was to dissuade voters from supporting pro-independence candidates.
"Mainland investment cases dropped significantly at that time of heightened tensions in the Taiwan Strait," Investment Commission deputy chief Huang Ching-tang said in an interview.
The commission, under the economics ministry, oversees inward and outward investments -- including those in China.
Some 30,000 Taiwan firms have poured more than US$20 billion into mainland China since a political thaw in the late 1980s, but the flow slowed in 1996.
From January to October, the number of new Taiwan-funded mainland investments fell 23 percent from the same 1995 period, while the invested amount rose 12 percent to US$1.021 billion.
Huang said this indicated small and mid-sized firms were losing their appetite for mainland investments and the accompanying political headaches.
"Two things have affected Taiwan's investment in the mainland -- relations across the Taiwan Strait and the government's policies (toward China)," he told Reuters.

Though the Investment Commission has not actively vetoed China projects, the government has openly expressed concern that Taiwan risked becoming too dependent on the economy of its arch rival -- and thus politically vulnerable.

Frustrated by a political impasse with China and a sagging domestic economy, President Lee Teng-hui and other leaders have tried to chill the "mainland fever" of Taiwan investors, urging firms to limit their economic links to China to avoid risky overdependence.
Many analysts expect Beijing to try to squeeze Taiwan for political concessions after mid-1997, when it gains control of Hong Kong, the island's main gateway to the China market.
The ruling Nationalist Party wants to develop Okinawa as an alternative to Hong Kong for handling mainland ties.
Taiwan's top economic policymaker in September urged local firms -- particularly powerful conglomerates -- to plough their profits back into Taiwan rather than China.
Chiang Pin-kung, chairman of the cabinet's Council for Economic Planning and Development, told local executives bluntly: "We should not put all our eggs in one basket."
The Investment Commission's Huang said comments by Lee and other officials had prompted some major Taiwan firms to reconsider their China ventures.
"Many companies, especially big enterprises, take their cue from the president's words. Mainland investments were down to a great extent in September and October," Huang said.
Taiwan investments in the mainland totalled US$46 million in September and US$64 million in October, compared with US$230 million in July and US$120 million in August, he said.
Two of Taiwan's biggest enterprises halted major projects.

Formosa Plastics Group announced in August, shortly after Lee's comments, that it was ending a deal to build what would have been the biggest Taiwan-funded project in China to date, a US$3 billion power plant in coastal Fujian province.

Food giant President Enterprises, already Taiwan's top China investor, said in September it had junked plans for a US$100 million mainland power station and instead would put more than T$30 billion (US$1.1 billion) in local projects over two years.
"From a businessman's point of views, the government's attitude is much more important than politics," said President Enterprises spokesman Yang Yu-pao.
"We need to comply with the government's policy."
Taipei has said it wanted Taiwan companies to keep their "roots" on the island.
"The mainland is one of the world's fastest growing areas. It's a trend that Taiwan companies will continue to invest there and the government cannot resist or block the trend," Huang said.
"But as long as companies make reciprocal investments at home while they invest in the mainland, Taiwan's economy will not be affected," he added.
"Our bottom line is that any mainland investment cannot violate national security and economic development," he added.
